槽形齊特琴以弦張於木槽開口發聲，音量可因槽形與弦架而偏小，常以葫蘆共鳴器放大，亦: The trough zither sounds from strings stretched across the opening of a wooden trough. The volume can be small, depending on the trough and the string holders, and is often boosted with a gourd resonator, or with a tin can. Pitch is set by tightening or loosening sections of string, and during playing the end of a string can be pressed to raise the pitch; the lowest string section gives the lowest note. Playing is mostly a repeating rhythmic melody, with no chords. Different forms — wide shallow bowl, long narrow shape, half-tube and flat-bottomed rectangle — produce different resonance and volume; the resonator can also be struck as a rhythm.
槽形齊特琴屬弦鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 315，見於東非與中非。: The trough zither is a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 315, found in East and Central Africa. The body is usually made from a single block of wood, shaped as a shallow bowl, a pot or a trough, with a slot or a hole at the end. Early strings were plant fibre or cattle tendon: one long string is threaded back and forth to make several sections, and the ends can be wound around wooden pegs. Notches and a wooden stick adjust the tension. The resonator is usually a gourd, sometimes a tin can; there may be a sound hole in the base. When the wood dried and split, it was reinforced with tin and nails, or bound with cord.
槽形齊特琴屬弦鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號 315，見於東非與: The trough zither is a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 315, found in East and Central Africa. To start, rest the wooden trough on your legs or beside you, hold the edge with one hand and pluck with the thumb or fingers of the other; it can also lie flat on a table and be played from above with both hands. The sound comes from the long strings crossing the opening, and a gourd resonator can be attached to increase the volume. Tune by adjusting the tightness of the string sections; during playing the end of a string can be pressed to raise the pitch. The usual practice is not to play chords but to repeat a rhythmic melody, and the player may sing while playing.
槽形齊特琴是非洲弦鳴樂器，屬齊特琴類，Hornbostel–Sachs編號315: The trough zither is an African chordophone of the zither family, Hornbostel–Sachs 315. The body is usually a shallow wooden trough, dish or bowl, with the strings stretched across the opening, often with a gourd or tin can as resonator. The player rests the instrument on the legs or beside the body and plucks with fingers or thumbs, repeating a rhythmic melody, and may sing while playing; the Acholi also use it to accompany dancers. Its range covers the borderland of East and Central Africa, including Rwanda, Burundi, Tanzania and Uganda.

The trough zither is an African chordophone of the zither family, Hornbostel–Sachs 315. The body is usually a shallow wooden trough, dish or bowl, with the strings stretched across the opening, often with a gourd or tin can as resonator. The player rests the instrument on the legs or beside the body and plucks with fingers or thumbs, repeating a rhythmic melody, and may sing while playing; the Acholi also use it to accompany dancers. Its range covers the borderland of East and Central Africa, including Rwanda, Burundi, Tanzania, Uganda and the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo.
槽形齊特琴的實際演奏場合，主要見於東非與中非的獨奏伴奏與節奏性合奏。來源提到，演: In practice the trough zither is heard mainly in solo accompaniment and rhythmic ensemble playing in East and Central Africa. Sources describe players accompanying song with a repeating rhythmic melody, without chords; in some traditions the instrument sits on the legs or beside the body and both hands pluck the high and low strings. In another way of playing, the instrument faces the player and the gourd resonator becomes a rhythm instrument, struck by a second person with the bare hands. It also serves as a fast rhythmic instrument, laying a repeating melodic beat for dancing.
槽形齊特琴起源於非洲中部和東部地區，尤其在盧旺達和布隆迪廣泛流傳。這種樂器的發展: The trough zither comes from Central and East Africa and is widespread in Rwanda and Burundi in particular. Its development is closely bound up with how local communities reworked and improved string instruments, and it reflects the deep roots of African craft and musical culture. Early makers used easily available natural materials such as wood and gourds, and refined the sound through long practice. Over time, craftsmen worked out five different trough designs and explored various resonators, among them the traditional gourd and the tin can introduced later. From its centre in Rwanda and Burundi the trough zither spread to other parts of East and Central Africa and became an important instrument of the region. That spread was shaped by geography and also reflects contact between different peoples. Today the trough zither is still a major representative of African traditional music, carrying deep historical and artistic value.
